overview: This map label covers 700 to 800 and a western Georgian footprint, not the unified kingdom established in 1008. Egrisi, Abkhazia and neighboring Kartli had different rulers and relationships with larger empires. The polygon includes Nokalakevi and Tsromi but excludes Tbilisi; eastern examples below supply context rather than extend its borders.

periods.title: Regional rulers between empires
periods.summary: Egrisi had shifted its allegiance in 697; Arab influence did not produce uniform control of the west.

periods.title: Campaigns and uneven authority
periods.summary: Marwan’s campaign of 735 to 736 strengthened Arab rule in eastern Georgia, while frontier regions followed different paths.

periods.title: A western kingdom emerges
periods.summary: Chronicles place Leo II’s consolidation of western Georgia in the 780s. The atlas endpoint is not its historical end.

items.text: In 697 Sergi, ruler of Egrisi, broke with Byzantium and aligned himself with the Arabs. Arab forces occupied Tsikhegoji, now Nokalakevi, and fortresses in the Kodori area, but soon left western Georgia. Allegiance could change faster than the walls surrounding a town.

Leo II’s family linked different political worlds: Christian chronicles describe his mother as a Khazar princess. They credit Khazar help with his consolidation of western Georgia in the 780s and release from Byzantine authority. This was a regional monarchy, not yet the later united Georgian kingdom.

The emerging kingdom was called Abkhazia, but its political name came to cover western Georgia more broadly. Its capital moved from Anakopia to Kutaisi. Those historical uses of "Abkhazia" should not be read as the boundaries of the modern region.

Where Arab authority operated in eastern Georgia, people faced land and personal taxes, support for soldiers and officials, and obligations to maintain roads and bridges. Government reached daily life through work and payments as well as battles; these obligations cannot simply be assigned to every household inside the western polygon.

At Nokalakevi, sixth to eighth-century buckles, clasps and pins bring clothing into view even when cloth has vanished. Excavators found them in buildings, occupation layers and graves, mostly inside the lower town’s defenses. Small fasteners are useful clues: sometimes the most ordinary part of an outfit survives longest.

Some of those accessories have parallels around the Black Sea, the Caucasus, the Danube, the Volga and the Eurasian steppe. Researchers consider both exchange and the movement of people serving in Byzantine armies. A matching buckle is a clue to connections, not a passport naming its wearer.

Two Nokalakevi people dated to the seventh century or the early eighth century left chemical clues in their bones. Carbon and nitrogen measurements suggest varied plant foods and a contribution from meat or dairy. The analysis describes broad diet patterns; it cannot tell us what either person ate for breakfast.

Potters kept supplying Nokalakevi after its busiest late antique centuries. Ceramic groups dated broadly from the seventh to eleventh centuries include pots with deep dimples or incisions, and thin, hard, white-clay vessels with polished surfaces, sometimes decorated in red. These fragments reveal continued local activity across political upheavals.

Nokalakevi’s inhabitants inherited imposing fourth to sixth-century defenses around a lower town and a high citadel. A tunnel led down to the Tekhuri River. Secure access to water was a practical part of a defended settlement: walls alone could not fill a bucket.

The same town preserves older bathing infrastructure. Two pipes passing through a substantial wall and waterproof mortar led excavators to identify a reservoir supplying a fifth or sixth-century bathhouse downslope. This is evidence for engineered water delivery before the map period, not proof that every eighth-century home had plumbing.

Tsromi’s early seventh-century church offered a striking shared interior: four freestanding piers supported its dome, while an upper gallery stood above the western entrance area. Deep triangular niches shaped the eastern facade. Builders were experimenting with arrangements that became important in later Georgian church design.

Inside Tsromi, mosaics and painted figures worked together: Christ and angels appeared above the Virgin and apostles. An inscription invoking Saint Rajden is dated by its letter forms to the eighth century. These surviving details show how inherited architecture continued to carry local acts of devotion.

sections.title: Skilled hands, learning and a written voice

items.text: Abo, an Arab artisan from Baghdad, was skilled in mixing myrrh and entered the service of Nerse, Kartli’s ruling prince. His story takes him through Kartli and the Khazar realm before his execution for his Christian conversion in 786. This named worker belongs to the wider eastern context around Tbilisi, outside the drawn polygon.

Between 786 and 790, John Sabanisdze composed Abo’s life at the request of Catholicos Samoel, preserving their letters as a preface. This gives us a concrete example of learned writing and church patronage. The work survives through later manuscript transmission, including a tenth-century witness, rather than the author’s original pages.

A short Georgian voice survives on Tsromi’s south facade: "Ⴜ(ႫႨႣႠ)Ⴍ ႤႩ(ႪႤႱႨ)ႠႭ" ,  ts’midao ek’lesiao, "Holy Church." This Asomtavruli-script inscription belongs to the church’s 620s to 630s construction, before the map interval. Parentheses mark letters expanded in the scholarly transcription; the full prayer asks mercy for Stephanoz Vipatos.

Archaeologists once considered a hurried Nokalakevi burial a casualty of the Persian attack of 551. Radiocarbon testing instead placed that person between 660 and 770. An eighth-century Arab attack is possible, but unproven. Scientific dating can overturn an attractive story without supplying a new culprit.

Families also left evidence beyond grand churches. A child, probably younger than six, was buried near ordinary building remains about 100 meters from Nokalakevi’s cemetery. The burial dates to 610 to 690, shortly before this card’s period. It reveals a different burial location, while the family’s reasons remain unknown.

ending.text: The year 800 ends this atlas record, not Georgian society. Around the eighth to ninth-century transition, regional powers including Abkhazia, Kakheti, Hereti and Tao-Klarjeti developed along different paths. Their later history belongs to the formation of new principalities and kingdoms, not the fall of one continuous eighth-century Georgian state.
